en: Which word fills the gap? “The girl ___ won the race is my cousin.”
Which word fills the gap? “The book ___ I borrowed was brilliant.”
Which word fills the gap? “That is the park ___ we play football.”
Which word fills the gap? “This is the boy ___ bike was stolen.”
We use “whose” to show that something belongs to someone.
Which word fills the gap? “Our car, ___ is very old, still runs well.”
Which word fills the gap? “Mr Ali, ___ teaches us maths, plays the guitar.”
Which word fills the gap? “The town ___ my gran lives is by the sea.”
Which word fills the gap? “I met a woman ___ dog can do tricks.”
We use “whose” to show that something belongs to someone.
Which word fills the gap? “The cake ___ Dad baked was delicious.”
Which word fills the gap? “The children ___ sang in the show got a prize.”
Which word fills the gap? “That is the shop ___ I bought my trainers.”
Which word fills the gap? “The artist ___ paintings we saw is famous.”
We use “whose” to show that something belongs to someone.
Which word is the relative pronoun in “The owl that lives in the barn hoots at night”?
“That” starts the relative clause, which tells us more about the owl.
Which word is the relative pronoun in “I have a friend who speaks three languages”?
“Who” starts the relative clause, which tells us more about the friend.
Which part is the main clause in “Although it was raining, we went to the park”?
“We went to the park” makes sense on its own, so it is the main clause.
Which part is the subordinate clause in “I brushed my teeth before I went to bed”?
“Before I went to bed” does not make sense on its own, so it is the subordinate clause.
Which part is the subordinate clause in “When the bell rang, everyone ran outside”?
“When the bell rang” needs the rest of the sentence to make sense, so it is subordinate.
Which sentence contains a subordinate clause?
We stayed inside because it was cold.
“Because it was cold” is a subordinate clause. It adds a reason to the main clause.
Which word can start a subordinate clause?
“Because” is a subordinating conjunction. “And” and “but” join two main clauses.
Which is the main clause in “The cat, which was very hungry, ate all its food”?
The cat ate all its food
Take out the relative clause and “The cat ate all its food” still makes sense on its own.
Which of these is a main clause that makes sense on its own?
“The bus was late.” is complete. The others leave you waiting for more.
Which part is the relative clause in “The boy who lives next door has a puppy”?
A relative clause starts with a relative pronoun such as “who” and tells us more about a noun.
Which part is the relative clause in “Paris, which is in France, is a big city”?
“Which is in France” starts with “which” and adds extra information about Paris.
Which sentence uses the correct relative pronoun?
The man who fixed our roof was kind.
The man which fixed our roof was kind.
The man whose fixed our roof was kind.
The man is a person, so we use “who”.
Which sentence uses the correct relative pronoun?
This is the café where we had lunch.
This is the café who we had lunch.
This is the café whose we had lunch.
A café is a place, so we use “where”.
Which sentence uses the correct relative pronoun?
I like the coat which has a hood.
I like the coat who has a hood.
I like the coat whose has a hood.
A coat is a thing, so we use “which”.
Which word fills the gap? “My friend Jo, ___ mum is a nurse, came to tea.”
We use “whose” to show that something belongs to someone.
Which word fills the gap? “The fox ___ we saw last night ran across the road.”
The fox is an animal, not a place or an owner, so “which” fits.
Which part is the subordinate clause in “If you finish early, you can read a book”?
“If you finish early” does not make sense alone, so it is the subordinate clause.
Which sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause?
I smiled when I saw the rainbow.
“When I saw the rainbow” is a subordinate clause added to the main clause “I smiled”.

en.title: Clauses and relative pronouns
en.teach: A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause does not (because it was cold). Relative pronouns start relative clauses: who for people, which for things, where for places, whose for belonging, and that.
